slides.title: Learning intention and success criteria
body: We are learning to collect numerical data and interpret centre and spread.
I can identify variable type, calculate mean, median, mode and range, and explain which summaries are meaningful in context.
slides.teacherNotes: Begin with examples of counts and measurements from the classroom and require units for every continuous variable.
slides.expectedResponse: Students distinguish counting from measuring and interpret each statistic as a feature of the data rather than a detached calculation.
slides.misconceptionResponse: Rounding a measured time to whole seconds does not turn time into a count.
slides.remediation: Ask whether a more precise measuring instrument could record values between the displayed numbers.

slides.title: Concept refresher and visual clues
body: Mean equals the sum divided by the number of values, and median requires ordered data.
Mode identifies the most frequent value, while range equals maximum minus minimum.
An outlier can affect mean and range much more than median, so interpret several distribution features together.
slides.teacherNotes: Link each statistic to a different question about the same data set before performing calculations.
slides.expectedResponse: Students explain that measures of centre describe location while range describes spread.
slides.misconceptionResponse: Range is not a typical value because it is a difference between endpoints.
slides.remediation: Mark the centre values and endpoint values in different positions on an ordered number line.

slides.title: Guided example: summarise 4, 5, 5, 7 and 9.
body: The ordered data total 30 across 5 observations.
The mean is 30 divided by 5, which equals 6.
The median is the middle value 5, and the mode is the repeated value 5.
The range is 9 minus 4, which equals 5.
slides.teacherNotes: Keep the ordered data visible and point to the values used in each calculation.
slides.expectedResponse: The mean is 6, the median is 5, the mode is 5 and the range is 5.
slides.misconceptionResponse: The range is 5 rather than 9 because spread is maximum minus minimum.
slides.remediation: Write the range calculation explicitly beneath the two endpoint values.

slides.title: 60-second Quick Check / Turn and Talk
body: For the data 6, 7, 7, 8 and 12, calculate the mean, median, mode and range.
Tell a partner which statistic is most affected by the value 12.
slides.teacherNotes: Look for an ordered-data method and listen for a distinction between the effect on mean or range and the stable median.
slides.expectedResponse: The mean is 8, the median is 7, the mode is 7 and the range is 6; the value 12 has a strong effect on the mean and range.
slides.misconceptionResponse: The median is 7 because it is the third ordered value, not the arithmetic average of all five values.
slides.remediation: Circle the middle position for the median and separately add all values for the mean.

practiceSheet.title: Acquiring Numerical Data and Measures of Centre Practice Sheet

questions.prompt: Classify the number of siblings each student has as a discrete or continuous numerical variable.
questions.answer: The number of siblings is a discrete numerical variable.
questions.summary: Siblings are counted in separated whole-number outcomes.
questions.hint: Decide whether the value is counted or measured on a scale.

questions.prompt: Classify each student's arm span measured in centimetres as a discrete or continuous numerical variable.
questions.answer: Arm span is a continuous numerical variable, even if it is rounded to the nearest centimetre.
questions.summary: Length is measured and can take values between recorded whole centimetres.
questions.hint: Ask whether a more precise instrument could produce a value such as 151.4 centimetres.

questions.prompt: Find the median and range of 3, 8, 5, 11 and 8.
questions.answer: After ordering the data as 3, 5, 8, 8, 11, the median is 8 and the range is 8.
questions.summary: The middle ordered value gives the median and 11 minus 3 gives the range.
questions.hint: Order the five values before selecting the middle and subtracting the endpoints.

questions.prompt: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of 2, 4, 4, 6, 9 and 11.
questions.answer: The mean is 6, the median is 5, the mode is 4 and the range is 9.
questions.summary: The sum 36 divided by 6 gives 6, the middle pair averages to 5, 4 repeats, and 11 minus 2 gives 9.
questions.hint: Use separate lines for total and count, middle pair, frequency and endpoints.

questions.prompt: The waiting times 3, 4, 4, 5 and 19 minutes include one extreme value; compare the mean and median and choose the better typical value.
questions.answer: The mean is 7 minutes and the median is 4 minutes, so the median better represents the cluster from 3 to 5 minutes while 19 should be reported as an extreme value.
questions.summary: The high value pulls the mean away from most observations but does not move the middle ordered value as far.
questions.hint: Calculate both centres and compare each with the four closely grouped times.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet contains masses recorded as 42 grams, 0.045 kilograms, 47 grams, a blank cell and 44 grams; identify two data-cleaning actions required before calculating a mean.
questions.answer: Convert all masses to one unit and investigate or mark the missing value rather than treating the blank as zero.
questions.summary: Consistent units and explicit handling of missing data are necessary for a meaningful calculation.
questions.hint: Check whether every entry uses the same scale and whether every participant has a valid measurement.

questions.prompt: A class's daily message counts have mean 12 and range 20; explain what each statistic communicates and one fact it does not reveal.
questions.answer: The mean communicates an average of 12 messages and the range communicates a 20-message gap between maximum and minimum, but neither reveals the complete distribution or where values cluster.
questions.summary: Centre and spread answer different questions and do not replace the original distribution.
questions.hint: Describe one location feature, one endpoint difference and one pattern that both summaries omit.

questions.prompt: Construct two five-value data sets that both have mean 6 and range 8 but have different medians, and verify the conditions.
questions.answer: One valid pair is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 2, 3, 5, 10, 10; both total 30 for mean 6, both have range 10 minus 2 equals 8, and their medians are 6 and 5 respectively.
questions.summary: Equal mean and range do not force equal middle positions, as the verified totals, endpoints and medians show.
questions.hint: Fix the endpoints at 2 and 10, make all five values total 30, and change the third ordered value.

questions.prompt: Plan how to acquire reliable continuous data about Year 7 reaction times, including units, precision and two quality checks before calculating summaries.
questions.answer: Use the same digital timer and procedure for every student, record reaction time in seconds to the same precision, repeat or flag impossible readings, check missing and duplicate entries, and then calculate and interpret centre and spread with the sample size stated.
questions.summary: A standard measurement procedure and transparent cleaning protect the meaning of later numerical summaries.
questions.hint: Specify how every measurement is made and how you will detect inconsistent, missing or impossible values.

identity.subject: Mathematics
identity.title: Numerical Data Displays and Distribution Comparison
identity.description: create different types of numerical data displays including stem-and-leaf plots using software where appropriate; describe and compare the distribution of data, commenting on the shape, centre and spread including outliers and determining the range, median, mean and mode.

topic.learningIntention: We are learning to construct and compare numerical data displays, including stem-and-leaf plots, and interpret distributions in context.
successCriteria: I can construct a stem-and-leaf plot with ordered leaves, a title and an unambiguous key.
I can recover original values and calculate centre and spread from a numerical display.
I can compare two distributions using evidence about centre, spread, clusters, gaps and extreme values.
deepDive: A numerical data display should make the distribution visible without changing the values it represents. A stem-and-leaf plot separates each value into a leading stem and a final leaf, preserves individual observations, and requires ordered leaves and a key such as 4 | 7 = 47 so the scale cannot be misread.

Centre describes where a distribution is located, spread describes how widely its values vary, and shape includes clusters, gaps, symmetry or a longer tail. Reading only a median or only the tallest stack can hide important differences between distributions.

A comparison must use the same variable, units and scale and must connect numerical evidence to context. Two groups can have the same median but very different ranges or clustering, so a strong conclusion cites at least one measure of centre and one feature of spread or shape.

vocabulary.definition: A distribution is the pattern formed by all values of a numerical variable, including its centre, spread and shape.
A stem-and-leaf plot separates leading digits from final digits while preserving each original numerical value.
A cluster is a region of a distribution where several values are concentrated.
Skew is asymmetry in a distribution with a longer tail towards lower or higher values.

misconceptions.idea: Leaves can be written in the order in which the data were collected.
misconceptions.correction: Leaves should be ordered within each stem so that the median, gaps and shape can be read reliably.

misconceptions.idea: A stem-and-leaf plot does not need a key because the digits are visible.
misconceptions.correction: A key is essential because the same marks could represent ones, tenths or another place-value scale.

misconceptions.idea: Two distributions with the same median must be practically the same.
misconceptions.correction: Equal medians can occur with very different ranges, clusters, gaps and extreme values.

workedExamples.title: Reading centre and spread from a stem-and-leaf plot.
steps: Use the key 4 | 7 = 47 and read the ordered rows 3 | 2 5 8, 4 | 1 3 3 7 9, 5 | 0 4 6 and 6 | 2 as twelve values.
The sixth and seventh values are 43 and 47, so the median is their mean, 45.
The minimum is 32 and the maximum is 62, so the range is 62 minus 32, which equals 30.
The value 43 occurs twice while every other value occurs once, and most observations lie in the 40s and 50s.
workedExamples.answer: The distribution has median 45, range 30, mode 43 and a concentration of values in the 40s and 50s.
workedExamples.check: Reconstructing all twelve values in order confirms the middle pair, endpoints and repeated value.

workedExamples.title: Comparing groups with equal medians but different spread.
steps: Group A has values 32, 40, 45, 47, 47, 50 and 62, while Group B has 40, 44, 46, 47, 48, 50 and 54.
Both groups have seven values and the fourth value is 47, so both medians are 47.
Group A has range 62 minus 32 equals 30, while Group B has range 54 minus 40 equals 14.
Conclude that the groups share the same centre by median, but Group B is more tightly clustered and Group A is much more variable.
workedExamples.answer: Both medians are 47, but Group A has range 30 and greater spread, whereas Group B has range 14 and stronger clustering around the high 40s.
workedExamples.check: The comparison uses the complete ordered values and reports both a centre feature and a spread feature in the same units.

slides.title: Learning intention and success criteria
body: We are learning to construct numerical displays and compare distributions using evidence.
I can make and read a keyed stem-and-leaf plot and describe centre, spread and shape in context.
slides.teacherNotes: Build one stem row from unsorted data and ask why ordering leaves changes readability without changing the data.
slides.expectedResponse: Students reconstruct values correctly and support comparisons with more than one distribution feature.
slides.misconceptionResponse: A display is not complete when its scale or units cannot be recovered from a key and labels.
slides.remediation: Ask the student to read one plotted mark as a full value and add the information needed to make that reading unambiguous.

slides.title: Concept refresher and visual clues
body: Write stems in order, place every leaf beside the correct stem, order the leaves and include a key.
Use median or mean for centre and range plus clusters, gaps or extremes for spread and shape.
Compare distributions only after checking that variable, units and display scale are compatible.
slides.teacherNotes: Use the comparison table to model a sentence that includes both similarity and difference.
slides.expectedResponse: Students state that equal centre does not imply equal spread or shape.
slides.misconceptionResponse: One shared statistic cannot establish that two full distributions are alike.
slides.remediation: Cover the medians and ask students to compare the endpoints and concentration of values first.

slides.title: Guided example: interpret the displayed stem-and-leaf plot.
body: The key 4 | 7 = 47 shows that stems are tens and leaves are ones.
There are twelve values, so average the sixth value 43 and seventh value 47 to obtain median 45.
Subtract minimum 32 from maximum 62 to obtain range 30, and identify 43 as the mode.
Most values lie in the 40s and 50s, so report that concentration together with the numerical summaries.
slides.teacherNotes: Number the ordered leaves cumulatively so the two middle positions are visible and then return to the contextual distribution language.
slides.expectedResponse: The plot has median 45, range 30, mode 43 and most values in the 40s and 50s.
slides.misconceptionResponse: With twelve observations, the median is the mean of positions six and seven rather than either one alone.
slides.remediation: Rewrite the leaves as one ordered list and mark the two central positions.

slides.title: 60-second Quick Check / Turn and Talk
body: A stem-and-leaf plot has key 2 | 1 = 21 and rows 2 | 1 4 8 and 3 | 0 5; find its median.
Tell a partner how the key determines the five original values.
slides.teacherNotes: Require students to reconstruct 21, 24, 28, 30 and 35 before naming the median.
slides.expectedResponse: The median is 28 because the ordered values are 21, 24, 28, 30 and 35.
slides.misconceptionResponse: The middle leaf 8 represents 28 rather than 8 because it must be combined with stem 2.
slides.remediation: Write each stem beside each of its leaves to rebuild the full values.

questions.prompt: In a stem-and-leaf plot with key 4 | 7 = 47, what value is represented by 5 | 3?
questions.answer: The entry 5 | 3 represents 53.
questions.summary: The stem gives the tens digit and the leaf gives the ones digit under the stated key.
questions.hint: Use the example key to combine stem 5 with leaf 3 in the same place-value pattern.

questions.prompt: Write the values represented by the row 3 | 2 5 8 when the key is 3 | 2 = 32.
questions.answer: The row represents 32, 35 and 38.
questions.summary: Each leaf is paired with the common stem to reconstruct one original value.
questions.hint: Keep the stem digit 3 and attach each leaf in turn.

questions.prompt: A student leaves each stem's leaves in collection order. Explain why the leaves should instead be ordered.
questions.answer: Ordered leaves allow the data to be read in numerical order so the median, clusters, gaps and extremes can be identified accurately.
questions.summary: Ordering improves interpretation without changing any observation.
questions.hint: Think about which distribution features depend on knowing the order of values.

questions.prompt: Construct a stem-and-leaf plot for 21, 24, 24, 29, 31, 35 and 38 using tens as stems, and include a key.
questions.answer: The plot has rows 2 | 1 4 4 9 and 3 | 1 5 8, with a valid key such as 2 | 1 = 21.
questions.summary: Every value appears once with ordered leaves beside its tens stem and an unambiguous key.
questions.hint: Group values by tens digit, order each set of ones digits and then state how one mark is read.

questions.prompt: For the ordered stem-and-leaf values 12, 15, 18, 21, 23, 23, 27 and 30, calculate the median, mode and range.
questions.answer: The median is 22, the mode is 23 and the range is 18.
questions.summary: The median averages 21 and 23, the repeated value is 23, and 30 minus 12 equals 18.
questions.hint: There are eight values, so use the middle pair before checking repetitions and endpoints.

questions.prompt: Class A has median 47 and range 30, while Class B has median 47 and range 14 for the same test; write a supported comparison.
questions.answer: The classes have the same centre by median, but Class B's scores are less spread out because its range is 16 points smaller.
questions.summary: A sound comparison distinguishes the shared centre from the different spread.
questions.hint: Use one sentence for the equal medians and another clause for the ranges.

questions.prompt: A student creates the row 4 | 9 1 7 3 with key 4 | 1 = 41; identify the presentation error and correct the row.
questions.answer: The leaves are unordered, so the corrected row is 4 | 1 3 7 9.
questions.summary: Leaves must increase from left to right within a stem.
questions.hint: Arrange the ones digits in numerical order while keeping the same stem.

questions.prompt: Compare Group A values 32, 40, 45, 47, 47, 50, 62 with Group B values 40, 44, 46, 47, 48, 50, 54 using centre, spread and clustering.
questions.answer: Both groups have median 47, but Group A has range 30 and widely separated endpoints, whereas Group B has range 14 and is more tightly clustered from 40 to 54.
questions.summary: The groups share a median but differ substantially in variability and concentration.
questions.hint: Find the fourth value and endpoint difference for each group before describing where most values sit.

questions.prompt: Two stem-and-leaf plots use identical rows, but Plot X has key 2 | 5 = 25 centimetres and Plot Y has key 2 | 5 = 2.5 metres; explain why their numerical patterns cannot be compared responsibly without conversion.
questions.answer: The keys use different scales and units, so every value must be converted to a common unit before centre, spread or contextual magnitude is compared.
questions.summary: Similar-looking marks can represent different quantities when keys and units differ.
questions.hint: Read one mark from each key as a full measurement and express both measurements in the same unit.

identity.subject: Mathematics
identity.title: Statistical Investigations and Sampling
identity.description: plan and conduct statistical investigations involving data for discrete and continuous numerical variables; analyse and interpret distributions of data and report findings in terms of shape and summary statistics.

topic.learningIntention: We are learning to plan and conduct statistical investigations and communicate findings that are justified by the sampled data.
successCriteria: I can write a statistical question and define its population, sample and numerical variable.
I can select a feasible sampling and data-collection method while identifying possible bias and nonresponse.
I can analyse a distribution and write a contextual conclusion with appropriate limitations.
deepDive: A statistical investigation begins with a question that anticipates variation, identifies the population of interest and defines a measurable numerical variable. The sample, measurement procedure and units must match that question so the collected data can actually address it.

A representative sample depends on selection method rather than size alone. Simple random or carefully implemented systematic sampling can reduce selection bias, while convenience and voluntary-response samples often over-represent accessible or strongly motivated people; nonresponse can introduce further bias.

After collection, data are checked, displayed and summarised by centre, spread and shape before a conclusion is written in context. The conclusion should distinguish the observed sample from the broader population, disclose limitations and avoid causal language unless the investigation design supports cause.

vocabulary.definition: The population is the complete group about which an investigation seeks information.
A sample is the subset of the population from which data are actually collected.
Sampling bias is systematic over-representation or under-representation caused by the way a sample is selected or responds.
A statistical question is a question that expects variable data from a group or repeated process.

misconceptions.idea: A very large convenience sample must represent the population well.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing a biased sample's size does not repair the systematic exclusion or over-representation created by its selection method.

misconceptions.idea: The sample and population are interchangeable because both refer to people in the study.
misconceptions.correction: Data are observed from the sample and used cautiously as evidence about the larger population.

misconceptions.idea: An association found in a survey proves that one variable caused the other.
misconceptions.correction: An observational association can be influenced by other variables and does not by itself establish causation.

workedExamples.title: Planning an investigation of Year 7 travel times.
steps: Ask, 'How long does it usually take students in our Year 7 cohort to travel to school?' and define the population as all Year 7 students at the school.
Select a random sample from every Year 7 home group so that one accessible class does not dominate, and record travel time in minutes using the same wording and reference day.
Check missing, impossible and duplicate entries, then display the continuous numerical data and calculate an appropriate centre and spread.

If the sample has median 18 minutes, range 52 minutes and a longer upper tail, conclude that a typical sampled journey was about 18 minutes but travel times varied widely, without claiming an exact result for every student.
workedExamples.answer: The investigation links a variable statistical question to a distributed random sample, consistent collection, distribution analysis and a qualified conclusion about Year 7 travel times.
workedExamples.check: Every conclusion refers to the sampled travel-time data, reports variation and avoids extending the result beyond the defined school population.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a biased survey of physical activity.
steps: A student surveys 120 members of school sports clubs to estimate weekly activity for all 600 Year 7 students.
Although the sample is large, club membership makes highly active students more likely to be included, so the sample is a convenience sample with selection bias.
Improve the design by randomly selecting students from the full Year 7 roll, or by randomly sampling the same proportion from each home group, and follow up nonresponses consistently.
Report the sample size, response rate, activity distribution and remaining limitations before generalising cautiously to the Year 7 population.
workedExamples.answer: The sports-club survey cannot represent all Year 7 activity reliably, and a random sample from the full cohort with transparent nonresponse reporting is stronger.
workedExamples.check: The revised sampling frame gives every Year 7 student a known opportunity for selection rather than restricting selection to sports-club members.

slides.title: Learning intention and success criteria
body: We are learning to plan, conduct and communicate a complete statistical investigation.
I can connect the question, population, sample, variable, collection method, distribution and qualified conclusion.
slides.teacherNotes: Keep the investigation cycle visible and require students to explain how a weakness in one stage limits the later claim.
slides.expectedResponse: Students identify a valid population and variable, select a defensible sample and communicate findings no more broadly than the evidence allows.
slides.misconceptionResponse: A larger sample improves precision only when its selection process is not systematically biased.
slides.remediation: Ask who had no realistic opportunity to enter the sample and how their exclusion could change the data.

slides.title: Concept refresher and visual clues
body: Define the statistical question, population and numerical variable before selecting a sample.
Collect consistently, clean transparently and analyse centre, spread and shape in context.
Conclude with evidence, scope and limitations, and do not turn an observed association into an unsupported causal claim.
slides.teacherNotes: Compare the sampling-method table by asking whose experiences are likely to be over-represented or absent in each method.
slides.expectedResponse: Students evaluate sampling methods through representativeness, feasibility and likely sources of bias.
slides.misconceptionResponse: A census can still have missing or inaccurate responses, while a well-selected sample can provide useful evidence.
slides.remediation: Separate the number invited, number responding and method of selection in a simple audit table.

slides.title: Guided example: investigate Year 7 travel times.
body: Ask how long students in the school's Year 7 cohort usually take to travel to school, and define travel time in minutes as the variable.
Randomly sample students across every home group and use one consistent question and reference day.
Clean the data, then display and summarise centre, spread and shape.
A median of 18 minutes and range of 52 minutes support a conclusion about a typical sampled journey and wide variation, with sampling limits stated.
slides.teacherNotes: At each stage, ask how the decision supports the original question and what limitation remains.
slides.expectedResponse: The conclusion is that the sampled students typically travelled about 18 minutes but showed wide variation, and it is cautiously applied to the school's Year 7 cohort.
slides.misconceptionResponse: A median of 18 minutes does not mean every student or even most students travelled for exactly 18 minutes.
slides.remediation: Return to the distribution and distinguish a centre summary from the full set of observed values.

slides.title: 60-second Quick Check / Turn and Talk
body: A student asks only people waiting at the salad bar to name their favourite school lunch; identify the population, sample and likely bias, then propose one improvement.
Tell a partner why your improved selection method better matches the target population.
slides.teacherNotes: Listen for a distinction between all relevant students and the salad-bar customers who were actually approached.
slides.expectedResponse: If the target population is all school students, the sample is the salad-bar queue and it is biased towards students already choosing that food area; randomly sampling students across year groups would improve representation.
slides.misconceptionResponse: Asking everyone in one queue is still biased even if every person in that queue responds.
slides.remediation: Circle the words 'all school students' and list which groups could never appear in the queue-based sample.

practiceSheet.title: Statistical Investigations and Sampling Practice Sheet

questions.prompt: Which is a statistical question: 'How many minutes do Year 7 students at this school spend reading on a weekday?' or 'How many minutes did Amira read yesterday?', and why?
questions.answer: The Year 7 question is statistical because it expects varying numerical responses from a group, while the question about Amira seeks one fixed value.
questions.summary: A statistical question anticipates variation across a population or repeated process.
questions.hint: Choose the question that would produce a distribution rather than one answer.

questions.prompt: In a survey of 80 randomly selected students from all 620 students at a school, identify the population and sample.
questions.answer: The population is all 620 students at the school, and the sample is the 80 randomly selected students.
questions.summary: The population is the target group and the sample is the subset that supplies data.
questions.hint: Separate the group the conclusion concerns from the group actually surveyed.

questions.prompt: A study records each student's journey time to school in minutes; classify the variable as discrete or continuous and justify your answer.
questions.answer: Journey time is continuous because time is measured on a scale, even if the recorded minutes are rounded.
questions.summary: Measurement remains continuous when reported to limited precision.
questions.hint: Ask whether a more precise clock could record values between whole minutes.

questions.prompt: A school surveys the first 100 students entering the library about weekly reading time; identify the likely sampling bias.
questions.answer: The convenience sample is likely to over-represent students who use the library and may read more than students who do not enter it.
questions.summary: The selection location systematically changes which students can enter the sample.
questions.hint: Identify who is easy to reach and who has no chance to be selected.

questions.prompt: Put these investigation stages in a defensible order: analyse the distribution, define the question and population, collect data consistently, select a sample, clean the data, and communicate a conclusion.
questions.answer: The order is define the question and population, select a sample, collect data consistently, clean the data, analyse the distribution, and communicate a conclusion.
questions.summary: Each stage supplies trustworthy information needed by the next stage.
questions.hint: Begin with what you want to know and end with what the evidence allows you to say.

questions.prompt: A random sample of 50 Year 7 students has median travel time 16 minutes and range 48 minutes; write a cautious contextual conclusion.
questions.answer: For the sampled students, a typical travel time was about 16 minutes and travel times varied widely across a 48-minute range, but sampling uncertainty means the exact values may differ for the whole Year 7 cohort.
questions.summary: The conclusion interprets centre and spread while keeping its claim within the evidence's scope.
questions.hint: Mention both median and range and include language that distinguishes sample from population.

questions.prompt: A voluntary online survey receives 400 responses from 2,000 students; explain why the large response count does not remove possible bias.
questions.answer: Students who chose to respond may differ systematically from nonresponders, so voluntary-response bias can remain even with 400 responses.
questions.summary: Sample size does not correct a selection process that over-represents motivated respondents.
questions.hint: Compare people who decided to participate with those who ignored the survey.

questions.prompt: Design a feasible investigation of Year 7 sleep duration that states a statistical question, population, sample, variable, collection method and one limitation.
questions.answer: Ask 'How many hours do students in our Year 7 cohort usually sleep on a school night?', define all Year 7 students as the population, randomly sample students from every home group, collect self-reported hours for the same specified night, analyse the distribution, and acknowledge that recall and self-reporting may be inaccurate.
questions.summary: The plan aligns every investigation component and identifies a realistic measurement limitation.
questions.hint: Write one clause for each required component and make the reference night consistent for every sampled student.

questions.prompt: A survey finds that students reporting more exercise also report higher wellbeing; evaluate the claim 'exercise caused the higher wellbeing' and write a justified alternative conclusion.
questions.answer: The survey shows an association but cannot establish causation because other variables and self-selection may affect both measures, so a justified conclusion is that higher reported exercise was associated with higher reported wellbeing in this sample.
questions.summary: Observational survey evidence supports an association rather than an unqualified causal claim.
questions.hint: State exactly what the data move together with and identify what the study did not control or manipulate.
